For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.
author: Peiyao Liu, Hongtao Zhu, Sizhe Zhang, Yang Su, Zhenyu Zhao, Nan Chen

title: Nearly Tight Almost Sure Convergence Rates for the Last iterate of SGD
content:
arXiv:2611.24151v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the almost sure convergence of the last-iterate optimization error of Stochastic (sub)Gradient Descent (SGD) for convex objectives. For smooth objectives, we establish convergence rates of order $k^{-1/3}$ when a stationary minimizer exists, and $k^{-1/4}$ otherwise, up to polylogarithmic factors, where $k$ denotes the iteration counter. We further show that the latter rate extends to nonsmooth convex objectives. All these rates are achieved by deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Finally, we establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponents $-1/3$ and $-1/4$ are optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors, for the corresponding problem classes.
author: Weiming Ou, Andrea Paudice, Xiao Wang

title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
content:
arXiv:2611.24181v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.
author: Arya Mazumdar, Prateeti Mukherjee, Harsh Vardhan

title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
content:
arXiv:2611.24187v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.
author: Ziyue Kang, Zixi Qi, Yuchen Dai, Nana Lv, Xirong Cheng, Liang Liu, Ying Li, Haoyan Wei, Haiyang Yao

title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
content:
arXiv:2611.24206v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.
author: Philippe Forest, Giulia Lioi, Mai Pham Quyen, Alix Lamouroux, Javen Shi, Adrien Merlini

title: TableControl: Gesture Interaction Through Surface Vibrations
content:
arXiv:2611.24218v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Integrating gesture sensing into furniture offers a way to interact with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces. We present TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition with the complete processing pipeline running on a microcontroller. Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, the system combines signal acquisition and preprocessing with neural event detection and gesture classification. The resulting labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down gestures are transmitted to a host computer without streaming the underlying sensor signals. Visitors explore two example applications through hands-on interaction: an endless runner game and a physical table lamp with on/off and brightness control. A dashboard displays recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.
author: Florian Hettstedt, Andreas Erbsl\"oh, Gregor Schiele

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
content:
arXiv:2611.24228v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.
author: Shunxing Yan, Fang Yao

title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
content:
arXiv:2611.24240v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.
author: Kevin Zhai, Bian Sun, Zhenyi Wang, Song Wang

title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
content:
arXiv:2611.24272v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.
author: Gianluigi Pillonetto, Mauro Bisiacco

title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
content:
arXiv:2611.24301v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.
author: Zizhuo Fu, Haochen Huang, Shengxuan Qiu, Linye Wei, Ziyu Tang, Runsheng Wang, Meng Li

title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
content:
arXiv:2611.24313v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.
author: Stavros Damianakis, Konstantinos Psounis

title: RespCCT and FreqCCT: Compact, Explainable and Cost-Aware Convolutional Transformers for Multi-Class Respiratory Disease Classification
content:
arXiv:2611.24323v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Chest auscultation depends on the listener, and software that classifies lung sounds could give a second reading where trained listeners are scarce. The most accurate published classifiers fine-tune large pretrained networks, and their accuracy is rarely reported with running cost or paired statistics. This study makes three contributions. (i) It proposes RespCCT and FreqCCT, two compact convolutional transformers of 173,187 and 124,999 parameters that learn from random initialization on mel, constant-Q and cepstral images of 5 s frames from three public databases, ICBHI, KAUH and RD@TR, with 1,665 audio files in seven classes. (ii) It compares both models with five ImageNet-pretrained networks and larger distilled variants on one test set, using paired bootstrap intervals. (iii) It measures the cost of every pipeline stage on one CPU thread, tests whether attribution maps depend on the trained weights, and probes whether the learned features reveal the recording source. On the test fold, RespCCT reaches an accuracy of 98.13% and a macro F1 of 0.970, and FreqCCT reaches 97.58% and 0.951. Over five folds, RespCCT with three seeds reaches 97.65% and 0.959, and FreqCCT with one seed reaches 96.95% and 0.941. The two strongest pretrained networks reach a macro F1 of 0.984, whereas RespCCT needs 2.0 to 64.6 times less weight storage. Computing the three input images takes longer than running either model, and a linear probe identifies the source database with 0.958 accuracy. A team can weigh accuracy against storage and time before device testing.
author: Auntor Chakma, Mst. Farhana Akter, Abu Henaf Rashid Ahmad Mufti, Asmana Yasmin

title: Can Weight-Space Programming Alter Learned Ethical Priorities?
content:
arXiv:2611.24330v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We investigate whether a weight edit can alter how a model trades off honoring a commitment against benefiting more people. In a concept-supervised text model, we alter fitted choice weights so that the benefit required to override a formal pledge is larger than for an ordinary promise. Across six independently trained text readers, the edit selects the larger group in both orders on 100% of targeted ordinary conflicts and 83.3% of targeted formal conflicts. It preserves the source model's success rates on smaller conflicts and its factual accuracy. The remaining formal-conflict failures coincide with errors reading a beneficiary number. A separate classifier demonstrates why this distinction matters: reusing a factual answer passes an unconditional choice test but fails to preserve small-gap promises. In a YOLO11n pilot on COCO128, a bias edit increased small-target matches from 3/43 to 9/43, and an equivalent score calibration reproduced the retained detections. These exploratory results show a way to test selective changes to learned priorities in a model with an exposed trade-off mechanism. Whether the method can discover such changes in less structured language models remains open.
author: Kai Yi Ji

title: Exploring Daily Emotional Well-Being through Personalized Data Analysis
content:
arXiv:2611.24342v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This project analysed daily emotional well-being from a personalized perspective using records of emotional states and contextual information derived from daily life. It was based on the idea that well-being is not a fixed value, but varies from day to day, and can be better understood in relation to individual context and behaviour. The work is framed within the field of Data Science and focuses on emotional states at an individual level. The project focused on constructing an integrated daily dataset from multiple personal data sources and analysing emotional states. The distributions of emotional variables, their temporal evolution and the differences between users were studied, together with their variability over time. Personality and well-being questionnaires were also incorporated as stable references to better contextualize daily emotional results. A simple personalized recommendation approach was then developed by comparing similar days within each user, exploring how past contextual conditions relate to differences in the user's emotional state. Finally, machine learning techniques were used to evaluate whether daily contextual information contains signals that help distinguish between different types of days relative to a person's usual well-being. The project adopted an applied approach, with an exploratory scope focused on understanding patterns rather than building a fully predictive system. The results showed that emotional well-being is very personal and changes from day to day. General models had limited value, while personalized approaches captured these differences much better, highlighting the importance of analysing each person on their own terms.
author: Adriana Rodr\'iguez Rodr\'iguez

title: OCTR2A: Real-Time RGB-to-BEV Trajectory Projection and Forecasting at Urban Intersections
content:
arXiv:2611.24352v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Trajectory forecasting at urban intersections is often studied assuming that reliable bird's-eye-view (BEV) motion histories are available, which in practice requires costly resources such as LiDAR, aerial views, HD maps, or calibrated infrastructure. We address this upstream perception-to-forecasting problem by reconstructing and predicting agents' BEV trajectories only from paired opposite-corner RGB cameras mounted on existing urban infrastructure at variable heights at inference time. We introduce the Opposite-Corner Trajectory Reconstruction and Anticipation Architecture (OCTR2A), a modular pipeline integrating per-view detection with class refinement, geometric cross-camera matching, transformer-based BEV projection, and egocentric GRU forecasting, trained in cascade and mainly supervised with a soft multi-scale spatial-overlap loss. Since no public benchmark provides this sensing configuration, we introduce R3ST++, a Blender-based synthetic benchmark built from SIND trajectories that provides synchronized opposite-corner views, cross-view correspondences, and BEV ground truth, while also serving as a deployment-support simulator for site-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on these datasets show that, with 12 observed and 12 predicted frames at 10\,Hz, OCTR2A achieves projection~-~forecasting ADE/FDE of 0.144/0.140~-~0.154/0.241~meters in real time on a single consumer GPU. Evaluated on ground-truth BEV histories, the forecasting module improves over the strongest state-of-the-art methods on SIND by 66.7\%/41.7\% ADE/FDE. Transfer experiments on TUMTraf-V2X show that R3ST++ pretraining supports adaptation to real-world roadside domains with different sensing configurations.
author: Emanuele Iacobelli, Simone Teglia, Francesco Pro, Claudia Melis Tonti, Irene Amerini

title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
content:
arXiv:2611.24379v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.
author: Vedant Navale

title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training
content:
arXiv:2611.24436v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.
author: Riku Huttunen, Samu Kainulainen, Matias Rusanen, Sami Myllymaa, Juha T\"oyr\"as, Timo Lepp\"anen, Henri Korkalainen

title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
content:
arXiv:2611.24453v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: https://ukiyo23rui.github.io/auto-emergence-demo/.
author: Ruiji Yu, Gus Xia

title: Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach
content:
arXiv:2611.24466v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.
author: Jiahao You, Ziye Jia, Chao Dong, Qihui Wu, Zhu Han

title: Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention
content:
arXiv:2611.24479v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.
author: Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu

title: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
content:
arXiv:2611.24507v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: While the notions of sphere packing and sphere covering underlie the most widely used criteria for space-filling design in computer experiments, namely, the maximin and minimax approaches, they suffer from major drawbacks in high dimensions. First, when the dimension $d$ is very large, deploying a space-filling design requires an extremely large number of design points, making the very notion of a space-filling design questionable. Second, these two design characteristics are highly sensitive to boundaries, particularly when the design domain is a hypercube (the case considered in this paper), and especially to its vertices. This sensitivity is particularly acute when the design size is less than $2^d$. Instead of considering the maximin or minimax criterion, we consider here the quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube. This error has three key advantages: it accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point $U$ to the design, is less sensitive to boundary effects than the maximin and minimax criteria, and, thanks to Zador's celebrated theorem, enables a smooth and natural transition to uniform designs as the design size tends to infinity. Building on recent results on the construction of optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772) we propose a method to generate random designs of a given target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error. The support of the resulting distribution is then used to construct designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$. We demonstrate that, for moderate $n$, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well---and significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube. We also explain how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.
author: Luc Pronzato, Anatoly Zhigljavsky

title: Taming the Tails of Stochastic Gradient Descent in the Interpolation Regime
content:
arXiv:2611.24562v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we study stochastic gradient descent in the smooth interpolation regime, where the population objective shares a common minimizer with the sample losses. In contrast to prior work, which has largely focused on in-expectation analysis, we obtain high-probability convergence guarantees under the same assumptions. In the convex case, we prove a fast rate of order $\log(\beta^{-1}) \cdot n^{-1}$ after $n$ iterations, with failure probability at most $\beta$. In the strongly convex case, we derive a family of moment-based bounds of order $\beta^{-p} \cdot \exp(-\mathcal{O}(p \cdot n))$ for $p \in (0,1]$, and complement them with a matching lower bound showing that the corresponding deterioration in the exponential rate is essentially unavoidable. In both settings, our theoretical results are unified across a broad class of step-size schedules. Building on this analysis, we extend our results to a low-noise regime and to nonconvex objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition.
author: Leonardo Galli, Daniela Angela Parletta, Andrea Paudice

title: AGAMOTTO: An AI-Enabled Framework for Time-Critical Tactical Course-of-Action Evaluation and Generation
content:
arXiv:2611.24568v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Current command and control (C2) platforms lack integrated simulation capabilities that would allow commanders to dynamically explore courses of action (COAs) during live operations. This paper presents ongoing research and contributions to the development of AGAMOTTO (Advanced Guidance and Analytics for Military Operations, Tactical Threats, and Outcomes) as part of the overarching NGC2 program, which advances the Army's efforts to modernize C2 systems, such as the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK). The paper outlines the current design, preliminary findings, and the remaining research tasks, with an emphasis on how the completed work will support tactical decision-making in future time-constrained environments. While the full system is still under development, initial development and results demonstrate the feasibility of AGAMOTTO. Early experiments highlight both the potential benefits and practical constraints of deploying AI-enabled tools in operational settings, and introduce lessons learned and a viable training strategy to make AI-generated COAs feasible in tactical scenarios.
author: Matthew L. Corbett

title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
content:
arXiv:2611.24602v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.
author: Ivan Lee, Xingyu Xu, Yuejie Chi

title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
content:
arXiv:2611.24619v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
author: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David

title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
content:
arXiv:2611.24636v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
author: DiffuSpace Technical Team

title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Qu\'ebec French
content:
arXiv:2611.24699v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Qu\'ebec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Qu\'ebec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.
author: Eeham Khan, Richard Khoury, Leila Kosseim

title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
content:
arXiv:2611.24719v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/
author: Emad Aghajanzadeh, Bethany Anne Wong, Leonhard Kunze, Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Forstenh\"ausler, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann

title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
content:
arXiv:2611.24727v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.
author: Manuel Tiglio

title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
content:
arXiv:2611.24741v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.
author: Hiba Akhaddar, Peter Plantinga, Mirco Ravanelli, Tristan Glatard

title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation
content:
arXiv:2611.24747v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow this gap, we introduce three physically motivated augmentations of training data. Two improve generalization, namely exploiting the vehicle's left-right symmetry and emulating accelerometer bias. Combined, they reduce the error on the validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%. Contrary to common expectation, on the SUV the data-driven estimator trained with both augmentations matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same training data.
author: Hendrik Sch\"afke, Simon F. G. Ehlers, Thomas Seel, Askar Vagapov, Christoph Schweers, Ahmed Trabelsi, Daniel O. M. Weber

title: Learning the Anyon Atlas
content:
arXiv:2611.24752v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We extend our previous search for the modular data of topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions from 22 to 42 anyons, identifying 150,679 new modular data. We do so by adding to our algorithm three rejection gates, two of them based on logistic regression, that discard representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ unlikely to yield modular data. We estimate that roughly 80% of the modular data between ranks 23 and 42 has been identified after closing under known constructions. With this data, we find counterexamples to a conjecture of Geiko and Moore that the reality of the higher Gauss sums suffices for time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories, and propose a refined criterion. We demonstrate the scalability of this gated implementation by identifying prime modular data at rank 100 that is not realized by any Chern-Simons theory. The identified data through rank 42 has been made available at https://AnyonAtlas.org, to which further data will be added as it is found.
author: Jonah Berean-Dutcher, Clay Cordova, Julio Parra-Martinez, Richard Tuddenham, Zekai Zhu

title: Training-free motion statistics match self-supervised behavior encoders
content:
arXiv:2611.24792v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Self-supervised encoders for animal behavior are often trained on, or fed, hand-built movement features. We ask whether they beat those ingredients when compared fairly. A training-free representation, made of generic per-frame measurements summarized over fixed time windows and reduced with PCA, is compared with retrained and released encoders (BAMS, hBehaveMAE) under a preregistered protocol: frozen representations of equal size and one shared classifier. On CalMS21 it reaches 85.8 macro F1 against 82.4 for the best encoder, ties with four labelled videos, and leads when the annotator changes or new behaviors must be learned from a few videos; the reading holds for encoders retrained with three seeds. On the MABe22 mouse triplets it scores 83.7 against 80.3 for the released hBehaveMAE (gap +3.4, 95% interval +2.1 to +4.7). On a second species, the MABe22 fly groups, the same recipe scores 51.6 mean F1 over 50 tasks against 48.2 for BAMS, the best published method. On Shot7M2, the synthetic basketball benchmark built by hBehaveMAE's authors, it scores 68.8 against 64.7 for hBehaveMAE, the best method in that paper, though hBehaveMAE remains better on the shortest movements. Short time windows carry most of the result. Raw keypoints in each body's own frame, summarized over the same windows, already match or beat the encoders on both mouse datasets and on Shot7M2; on the fly groups they fall short, and the measurements add 5.3 points. On these benchmarks, current behavior encoders have yet to beat the hand-built features they learn from, and such baselines should be reported alongside them.
author: Ziwen Chen

title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
content:
arXiv:2611.24793v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.
author: Tobias Braun, Marcus Rohrbach, Lorenzo Cavallaro

title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems
content:
arXiv:2611.24839v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured.
  We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.
author: Tushin Mallick, Evan Rose, Matthew Laws, Alina Oprea, Cristina Nita-Rotaru

title: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving
content:
arXiv:2611.24840v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.
author: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo

title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
content:
arXiv:2611.24876v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.
author: Beyazit Yalcinkaya, Ethan Pronovost, Maximilian Naumann, Marcell Vazquez-Chanlatte

title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
content:
arXiv:2611.24908v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.
author: Samet Demir, Zafer Dogan

title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
content:
arXiv:2611.24932v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.
author: Priyanka Sinha, Sugam Pandey

title: Loss-Controlling Calibration with Asymptotic Guarantees
content:
arXiv:2301.04378v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We propose a learning framework for calibrating predictive models to perform loss-controlling prediction, which extends our proposed conformal loss-controlling prediction framework to more general settings. In contrast to existing methods, the predictors built by the proposed approach are not restricted to set-valued predictors, and the loss function can be any measurable function without requiring monotonicity assumptions. The approach is a natural extension of conformal loss-controlling prediction, since it reduces to the latter when the predictors are set-valued with the nesting property and the losses are monotone. The loss-controlling guarantee of the proposed framework is established in the asymptotic setting and is empirically verified in selective regression and high-impact weather forecasting, demonstrating its effectiveness for the domains requiring general loss-controlling prediction.
author: Di Wang, Yujin Li, Junzhi Shi, Pingping Wang, Shuo Zhuang, Hongyue Li

title: Survival of the Fittest Perturbations: Uncertainty-Aware Evolution of Adversarial Distributions for Robust Generalization
content:
arXiv:2411.02871v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Despite deep learning's broad successes across diverse scenarios, its vulnerability to adversarial examples impedes deployment, making adversarial training a leading approach to improve robustness. However, pointwise adversarial training maps each clean sample to a single adversary, overlooking surrounding adversarial variability and the associated shifts in feature statistics. To address these issues, we propose Evolutionary Uncertainty-Aware Distributional Adversarial Training (EvoUAD-AT). Specifically, we design an evolutionary adversarial uncertainty modeling module that maintains an instance-wise search distribution over adversarial feature statistics around an adversarially generated anchor. Candidates are evaluated under the current model, selected by their threat to a benign reference, and used to adapt the distribution; strategy parameters are retained across epochs. To avoid anchoring on misclassified clean samples, we refine the alignment reference and match benign and adversarial distributions. Introspective gradient matching further regularizes input gradients without external supervision. Our analysis characterizes the elite fitness surrogate and gives a conditional certificate for latent adversarial features. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both clean accuracy and robustness, with thorough analyses confirming the effectiveness of each proposed component.
author: Junhao Dong, Zicheng Yu, Xinghua Qu, Z. Jane Wang, Yew-Soon Ong

title: Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing: Early Stopping Overparameterized Diffusion Models
content:
arXiv:2505.16959v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models have become a cornerstone of modern generative AI, yet the mechanisms underlying their generalization remain poorly understood. In fact, if these models were perfectly minimizing their training loss, they would just generate data belonging to their training set, i.e., memorize, as empirically found in the overparameterized regime. We revisit this view by showing that, in highly overparameterized diffusion models, generalization in natural data domains is progressively achieved during training before the onset of memorization. Our results, ranging from image to language diffusion models, systematically support the empirical law that memorization time is proportional to the dataset size, consistent with a kernel-regression bound on the time required to fit the empirical score at low noise. Generalization vs. memorization is then best understood as a competition between time scales. We show that this phenomenology is recovered in diffusion models learning a simple probabilistic context-free grammar with random rules, where generalization corresponds to the hierarchical acquisition of deeper grammar rules as training time grows, and the generalization cost of early stopping can be characterized. We summarize these results in a phase diagram. Overall, our results support that a principled early-stopping criterion - scaling with dataset size - can effectively optimize generalization while avoiding memorization, with direct implications for hyperparameter transfer and privacy-sensitive applications.
author: Alessandro Favero, Antonio Sclocchi, Matthieu Wyart

title: Hyperparameter Optimization via Budget Allocation in Lipschitz Spaces
content:
arXiv:2510.10605v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hyperparameter optimization and model selection often require allocating a limited evaluation budget across many candidate configurations, where performance improves with additional training or resources. We study this setting when each configuration has an unknown performance curve over budget. Similarity between configurations induces similarity between their curves, capturing geometric structure in the search space. We formalize the resulting decision problem as Unknown Value Probing and propose budget allocation strategies that combine principled exploration of the configuration space with value-informed concentration on regions supported by observed evidence. We prove worst-case approximation guarantees for our approach and show these guarantees are near-optimal by matching corresponding hardness barriers. Extensive experiments on large benchmark suites spanning more than 250 experimental settings demonstrate consistent gains over strong baselines in both anytime behavior and final incumbent performance.
author: MohammadHossein Bateni, Hossein Esfandiari, Samira HosseinGhorban, Alireza Mirrokni, Radin Shahdaei

title: Assessing the robustness of heterogeneous treatment effects in survival analysis under informative censoring
content:
arXiv:2510.13397v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Dropout is common in clinical studies, with up to half of patients leaving early due to side effects or other reasons. When dropout is informative (i.e., dependent on survival time), it introduces censoring bias, because of which treatment effect estimates are also biased. In this paper, we propose an assumption-lean framework to assess the robustness of conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates in survival analysis when facing censoring bias. Unlike existing works that rely on strong assumptions, such as non-informative censoring, to obtain point estimation, we use partial identification to derive informative bounds on the CATE. Thereby, our framework helps to identify patient subgroups where treatment is effective despite informative censoring. We further propose a novel model-agnostic meta-learner, called SurvB-learner, to estimate the bounds that can be used in combination with arbitrary machine-learning models, and that has favorable theoretical properties such as double-robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. We finally demonstrate the effectiveness of our meta-learner across various experiments using both simulated and real-world data.
author: Yuxin Wang, Dennis Frauen, Jonas Schweisthal, Maresa Schr\"oder, Stefan Feuerriegel

title: Consecutive Preferential Bayesian Optimization
content:
arXiv:2511.05163v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Preferential Bayesian optimization allows optimization of objectives that are either expensive or difficult to measure directly, by relying on a minimal number of comparative evaluations done by a human expert. Generating candidate solutions for evaluation is also often expensive, but existing preferential optimization methods do not account for this production cost. We introduce Consecutive Preferential Bayesian Optimization (CPBO) for the consecutive setting, where production cost is reduced by reusing the previous candidate in each comparison. We also account for the perceptual ambiguity of the oracle providing the feedback by incorporating a Just-Noticeable Difference threshold into a probabilistic preference model to capture indifference to small utility differences. We adapt an information-theoretic acquisition strategy to this setting, selecting new configurations that are most informative about the unknown optimum under a preference model accounting for the perceptual ambiguity. We empirically demonstrate a notable increase in accuracy in setups with high production costs or indifference feedback, and demonstrate the practical feasibility of CPBO in a real-world food extrusion task.
author: Aras Erarslan, Carlos Sevilla Salcedo, Ville Tanskanen, Anni Nisov, Eero P\"aiv\"akumpu, Heikki Aisala, Kaisu Honkap\"a\"a, Arto Klami, Petrus Mikkola

title: CoreQ: Mismatch-Corrected Successive Rounding for LLM Quantization
content:
arXiv:2602.05902v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of large language models by mapping pretrained weights to low-bit formats without retraining, typically using a small calibration set to minimize a layer-wise calibration objective. However, this sequential procedure induces a mismatch: errors from earlier quantized layers alter the inputs received by later layers, causing the activations to deviate from those of the full-precision model. Recent approaches introduce mismatch-aware calibration objectives to compensate for this effect, but leave open how much of the observed mismatch should shift each layer's calibration target. We show that fully applying the empirical mismatch correction can overfit finite calibration data, while using a fixed correction coefficient ignores variation in mismatch estimates across layers. To address these limitations, we propose CoreQ, a learning-free PTQ framework that uses a geometric decomposition of the mismatch to compute a closed-form, layer-adaptive correction coefficient. This coefficient controls how much of the observed mismatch enters each layer's calibration target, reducing overfitting to limited calibration data without coefficient tuning. CoreQ then applies efficient greedy successive rounding to the resulting triangular least-squares objective. Its bounded beam-search extension, K-CoreQ, trades modest additional compute for improved performance. Across multiple LLM families, scales, bit-widths, and quantization settings, CoreQ and K-CoreQ achieve lower perplexity and higher downstream accuracy than strong PTQ baselines. Code is available at GitHub.
author: Seohyeon Cha, Huancheng Chen, Dongjun Kim, Haoran Zhang, Kevin Chan, Gustavo de Veciana, Haris Vikalo

title: Pragmatic Curiosity: A Unified Framework for Hybrid Learning and Optimization via Active Inference
content:
arXiv:2602.06104v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many engineering and scientific workflows rely on expensive black-box evaluations, requiring sequential decisions that must both improve task performance and reduce uncertainty. Bayesian optimization (BO) and Bayesian experimental design (BED) provide powerful but largely separate treatments of goal-directed optimization and information-seeking experimentation, leaving limited guidance for hybrid settings in which learning and optimization are intrinsically coupled. We propose Pragmatic Curiosity (PraC), a unified framework for hybrid learning and optimization via active inference. PraC evaluates candidate queries by trading information gain about a task-relevant latent symbol against an expected regret-based potential over outcomes. This formulation foregrounds three operational design choices: which latent quantity should be clarified, how task value is encoded as regret, and how strongly information gain should be exchanged against pragmatic regret. We instantiate PraC across three regimes of increasing complexity: decision-oriented monitoring with fixed global symbols and known downstream losses, targeted active search with induced local symbols and evolving coverage goals, and composite Bayesian optimization with hierarchical regret learning under unknown preferences. Across these regimes, PraC reduces downstream decision risk, improves coverage of critical outcome regions, and jointly learns predictive and preference structures without relying on task-specific staging rules.
author: Yingke Li, Anjali Parashar, Enlu Zhou, Chuchu Fan

title: Towards Generalizable Reasoning: Group Causal Counterfactual Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning
content:
arXiv:2602.06475v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at complex tasks with advances in reasoning capabilities. However, existing reward mechanisms remain tightly coupled to final correctness and pay little attention to the underlying reasoning process: trajectories with sound reasoning but wrong answers receive low credit, while lucky guesses with flawed logic may be highly rewarded, affecting reasoning generalization. From a causal perspective, we interpret multi-candidate reasoning for a fixed question as a family of counterfactual experiments. Building on this, we propose Group Causal Counterfactual Policy Optimization to explicitly train LLMs to learn generalizable reasoning patterns. It proposes an episodic causal counterfactual reward that jointly captures (i) robustness, encouraging the answer distribution induced by a reasoning step to remain stable under counterfactual perturbations; and (ii) effectiveness, enforcing sufficient variability so that the learned reasoning strategy can transfer across questions. We then construct token-level advantages from this reward and optimize the policy, encouraging LLMs to favor reasoning patterns that are process-valid and counterfactually robust. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate its advantages.
author: Jingyao Wang, Xingyu Zhang, Peizheng Guo, Jiahuan Zhou, Zhenghao Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Chuxiong Sun, Wenwen Qiang

title: Signature-Kernel Based Evaluation Metrics for Robust Probabilistic and Tail-Event Forecasting
content:
arXiv:2602.10182v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Standard sample-based metrics like Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) and Quantile Loss (QL) are frequently used in the evaluation of probabilistic time-series forecasting. However, these metrics fail to capture multivariate correlations or assess the ability to capture distribution tails. These global metrics are insensitive to errors on high-utility events in distributional tails due to over-representation of the distribution's body. To accurately measure distributional fidelity on tail-regions and regions of high utility while still having a proper scoring rule, we introduce a family of censored signature kernel metrics. Our proposed metrics concentrate evaluation of forecasts to a focus region, representing high-utility or distributional tails, by collapsing the body of the distribution to a single pivot. Our benchmarks on time-series foundation models (TSFMs) reveal that while a clear ranking can be formed for distribution capture, there is no clear winner for tasks like systemic load prediction. This indicates that models with a strong ability to capture an overall distribution do not produce forecasts with high downstream utility. To encourage the use of the proposed metrics we open-source the efficient signature kernel (ESK) library. This library facilitates batch computation, with custom triton kernels, achieving a speed-up of up to 3.58$\times$ compared to implementations via the popular SigKernel library. Code for our metrics are available on GitHub.
author: Benjamin R. Redhead, Thomas L. Lee, Peng Gu, V\'ictor Elvira, Amos Storkey

title: Counterfactual Feature Regularization for Expansion-Based Class-Incremental Learning
content:
arXiv:2603.09145v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Current expansion-based methods for Class Incremental Learning (CIL) effectively mitigate catastrophic forgetting by freezing old features. However, such task-specific features learned from the new task may collide with the old features. From a causal perspective, spurious feature correlations are the main cause of this collision, manifesting in two scopes: (i) guided by empirical risk minimization (ERM), intra-task spurious correlations cause task-specific features to rely on shortcut features. These non-robust features are vulnerable to interference, inevitably drifting into the feature space of other tasks; (ii) inter-task spurious correlations induce semantic confusion between visually similar classes across tasks. To address this, we propose a Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS)-based regularization method to guide feature expansion in CIL. Specifically, we first extend the definition of PNS to expansion-based CIL, termed CPNS, which quantifies both the causal completeness of intra-task representations and the separability of inter-task representations. We then introduce a dual-scope counterfactual generator based on twin networks to ensure the measurement of CPNS, which simultaneously generates: (i) intra-task counterfactual features to minimize intra-task PNS risk and ensure causal completeness of task-specific features, and (ii) inter-task interfering features to minimize inter-task PNS risk, ensuring the separability of inter-task representations. Theoretical analyses confirm its reliability. The regularization is a plug-and-play method for expansion-based CIL to mitigate feature collision.
